class: inverse, center, middle
name: changed

# What changed

---

# I last taught this class in 2021

The syllabus was a tooling course ([mkt615](https://github.com/dadepro/mkt-615))

Git. Shell. R. `data.table`. `ggplot2`. MySQL. Scraping.

--

The premise was that these tools were **hard to learn**, that nobody would teach you,
and that you would waste years of your PhD rediscovering them badly.

--

<br>

That premise was correct in 2021.

--

It is mostly wrong now.

---

# The cost of producing analysis has collapsed

You can now get a working merge, a panel construction, a fixed-effects regression,
and a publication-quality figure in a few minutes.

--

Not *good* versions of those things, necessarily. But running versions.

--

<br>

If I spend three hours teaching you `data.table` verbs, I am teaching you something you
can get from a model in nine seconds.

--

That is no longer where your time is best spent.

---

# But something else did not get cheaper

.large2[Knowing whether the analysis is **right**.]

--

<br>

Producing a regression table is now nearly free.

Knowing whether that table means what you think it means is exactly as hard as it was
in 2021 (perhaps harder).

--

<br>

The ratio between the cost of producing results and verifying them has moved by orders of
magnitude. That is one of the most important facts about doing empirical research right
now.

---

# The uncomfortable version

An LLM will write you code that:

- runs without error
- produces output that looks good
- silently drops 40% of your sample in a join
- and gives you a coefficient you will put in a paper

--

<br>

It will not tell you it did this. It does not know it did this.

--

<br>

.large2[**You are the only error-detection mechanism in the pipeline.**]

---

# So this course changed

The old constraint was **execution**: can you write the code at all?

The new constraint is **judgment**: should this code have been written, and is its
output correct?

--

<br>

Everything in the first seven weeks follows from that.

We still cover git, the shell, SQL, and data manipulation. But as *infrastructure for
catching errors*, not as syntax instruction. You will pick up syntax from the models.

---

# There is also genuinely new material

LLMs are not only tools for doing research. They are now **research instruments**.

--

People use them to:

- measure constructs from text, images, and audio at scale
- simulate survey respondents
- classify, annotate, and extract at a cost that makes new questions feasible

--

<br>

Each of these introduces statistical problems that need to be addressed.

Weeks 4 and 5 are about those problems. That is the methodological core of my half.

---

# Course overview

### (All this is in the [syllabus](https://github.com/dadepro/mkt699))

---

# Structure

I teach the **first seven weeks**. Professor Chen teaches weeks 8–15 on structural
estimation of choice models.

Each half is graded separately by the respective instructor. Your final grade is the
average.

--

<br>

We use Git and GitHub for everything: course material, assignments, your project.

Material lives at https://github.com/dadepro/mkt699

---

# The seven weeks

| Week | Topic |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | Reproducible research infrastructure |
| 2 | AI-assisted analysis and the verification problem |
| 3 | Data acquisition, storage, and provenance |
| 4 | LLMs as measurement instruments I: validation |
| 5 | LLMs as measurement instruments II: inference |
| 6 | Credibility: design, specification search, experiments |
| 7 | Project presentations |

---

# Grading (first half)

| | % |
|:--|--:|
| Semester project, presentation and report | 45% |
| Project milestones | 15% |
| 2 programming assignments | 20% |
| Paper presentation | 10% |
| Class participation | 10% |

---

# Logistics

**Class:** Wednesdays, 1:00–4:00 pm, HOH 706.

**Office hours:** right after class, or by appointment
([proserpi@marshall.usc.edu](mailto:proserpi@marshall.usc.edu)).

--

<br>

Come to office hours early in the semester rather than late. A project that is badly
scoped in Week 2 cannot be fixed in Week 6.

---

# How to read for this class

You will read up to four papers a week related to the topics we cover in class. If the paper is about a design, you should be able to answer the following questions:

1. What is the **estimand**? What number are they trying to learn?
2. What is the **identifying assumption**? What has to be true?
3. **What would break it?**

--

<br>

If you can answer these three, you have read the paper. If you can only summarize what
they did, you have not.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: project

# The project

---

# The semester project

Starting today, you develop an original empirical project that uses an LLM as a
**measurement instrument**. You present it in Week 7.

--

<br>

It should be scoped to be:

- small enough to finish in seven weeks
- large enough to potentially become a real paper

--

<br>

Most of you should aim for the second outcome. Some of you will get there.

---

# Requirements

Your project must:

1. Pose a question that **cannot** be answered with off-the-shelf structured data
2. Describe the data and state an **identification argument**: what variation identifies
   the estimand, and what would break it
3. Use an LLM to construct **at least one variable** from unstructured data
4. Include a **validation study** against human-labeled data, with the sampling scheme
   stated explicitly
5. Report downstream estimates with an appropriate **correction**, compared against the
   naive plug-in estimates
6. Be **fully reproducible** from your repository, with a documented AI-use log

---

# What that looks like

Use an LLM to measure something previously unmeasurable at scale, then use it to answer a
substantive marketing question.

--

<br>

*Examples: positioning language in product descriptions; the emotional content of service
interactions; visual attributes of listings; complaint taxonomies in reviews.*

--

<br>

The goal is to ensure that you understand the importance of validation and correction in the context of using LLMs for measurement.

---

# Milestones

.small90[
| Week | Date | Milestone |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Aug 26 | Repository initialized |
| 2 | Sep 2 | One-paragraph question, data source identified |
| 3 | Sep 9 | Data acquired, pipeline reproducible, identification drafted |
| 4 | Sep 16 | Measurement approach specified; validation designed |
| 5 | Sep 23 | Validation complete; naive estimates |
| 6 | Sep 30 | Corrected estimates; identification revised; robustness |
| 7 | Oct 7 | 20-minute presentation + short written report |
]

--

These milestones exist so that you cannot do this project in the last week
because a project done in the last week will not have a validation study, and a project
without a validation study is not a project.

---

# On null results

.large2[A well-designed project that finds nothing will get a **higher grade** than a
badly identified project that finds something.]

--

<br>


You are going to spend a career deciding whether to believe your own results. Start now.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: organization

# Project organization

---

# Why this matters more now, not less

The standard argument for reproducibility: other people should be able to check your
work, and *you* will need to rerun this in two years when a referee asks.

--

<br>

Both still true. But there is a new argument.

--

<br>

.large2[When a model writes your code, a reproducible pipeline is your **only**
mechanism for catching what it did wrong.]

---

# The new failure mode

You ask a model to "clean the data and run the regression."

It does. You get a number. The number is plausible. You move on.

--

<br>

Three weeks later you ask it to "add controls for market size."

It rewrites the cleaning step. Your sample changes. Your original number is no longer
reproducible, and **you do not notice**, because you never had a fixed pipeline in the
first place.

---

# Structure your project like this

```
my-project/
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          # never edited, never overwritten
│   └── clean/        # generated, disposable
├── code/
│   ├── 01-collect.R
│   ├── 02-clean.R
│   ├── 03-measure.R  # the LLM step
│   ├── 04-validate.R
│   └── 05-analysis.R
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
├── prompts/          # NEW: your measurement instruments
└── ai-log.md         # NEW: what you asked, what it did
```

---

# Two rules that will save you

**1. `data/raw/` is read-only.**

Never edit a raw file. Never overwrite one. Every transformation is a script that reads
from `raw/` and writes to `clean/`.

If you break this, you have lost the ability to reproduce anything.

--

**2. Everything in `clean/` and `output/` is disposable.**

You should be able to delete both directories entirely and rebuild them by running your
scripts in order.

If you cannot, you have a manual step you have forgotten about. And that step is where
your bug is.

---

# The two new directories

`prompts/` and `ai-log.md` are not in the standard reproducibility templates. They are
here because of what changed.

--

<br>

**`prompts/`** holds the exact prompts and model versions you used to generate any
variable that enters your analysis.

A prompt *is* a measurement instrument. An undocumented prompt is an unreproducible
instrument. You would not write "we surveyed some people somehow" in a paper.

--

**`ai-log.md`** records what you asked for, what you got, and, critically, what it got
wrong that you caught.

That last part is graded, and honest reporting helps your grade.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: git

# Version control

---

# Git, briefly

Some of you use git already. Some of you have never touched it. Both are normal in
your first two years.

I am not going to drill syntax. (ask a model, it is genuinely good at this). But I am
going to make sure you have the mental model, because that is the part models explain
badly.

--

<br>

I am going to tell you what git is **for** in this course:

.large2[It is how you find out what the model changed when you weren't looking.]

---

# The mental model

Three places your work lives. Almost every git confusion comes from not knowing which
one you are talking about.

--

.small90[
| Place | What it is |
|:--|:--|
| **Working directory** | The files as they are right now |
| **Staging area** | What you have marked to go in the next commit |
| **Repository** | The permanent history of commits |
]

--

<br>

`git add` moves working directory → staging.

`git commit` moves staging → repository.

---

# The commands you will use daily

```bash
git status                 # what is changed, what is staged
git diff                   # changes NOT yet staged
git diff --staged          # changes that ARE staged
git add code/02-clean.R    # stage one file
git add -A                 # stage everything
git commit -m "message"    # commit staged changes
git log --oneline          # history, compactly
```

--

<br>

`git status` is the answer to "what is going on." Run it constantly. It also tells you
what to do next, git is unusually good about this.

---

# The workflow that matters

```bash
# BEFORE you let an agent touch your code
git add -A && git commit -m "working state: baseline results"

# ... let the model do its thing ...

git diff HEAD    # <-- THIS. every time.
```

--

<br>

`git diff` is the highest-value command in your entire toolkit right now.

An agentic tool can touch fifteen files. It will summarize what it did. **The summary is
not the diff.** Read the diff.

---

# Reading a diff

```diff
--- a/code/02-clean.R
+++ b/code/02-clean.R
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@
   listings <- listings %>%
-    filter(price > 0)
+    filter(price > 0, price < 1000)
```

--

`-` is what was there. `+` is what replaced it.

--

<br>

That one-line change dropped every luxury listing from your sample. Nobody mentioned
it. It is one character short of invisible.

--

.large2[Knowledge of the diff is the key to understanding what has changed.]

---

# Commit discipline

Commit **before** every AI-assisted change, not after.

--

Your commit history becomes a set of restore points. When you discover on Thursday that
your coefficient changed on Tuesday, you can find the commit where it changed.

--

<br>

Commit often. A commit is free. A lost afternoon is not.

--

<br>

The habit to build: **commit whenever something works**, even if it is half-finished.
"Working state" is a perfectly good commit message.

---

# Write commit messages for future you

```bash
# useless
git commit -m "update"
git commit -m "fixes"
git commit -m "asdf"

# useful
git commit -m "Drop listings with price > 1000 (outlier trim)"
git commit -m "Switch clustering from city to tract level"
git commit -m "Add LLM sentiment measure, v2 prompt"
```

--

<br>

You are writing to the person who, in eight months, has to explain to a referee why the
sample size changed. That person is you, and they will not remember.

---

# Finding when things broke

Your coefficient changed and you don't know when.

--

```bash
git log --oneline                        # find candidate commits
git diff abc123 def456 -- code/02-clean.R  # compare two points
git log -p code/02-clean.R               # full history of ONE file
git log -S "filter(price"                # commits that touched this string
```

--

<br>

That last one, `git log -S`, searches history for when a piece of code appeared or
disappeared. It is how you find the commit that introduced a filter nobody remembers
adding.

---

# Undoing things

The three you actually need:

```bash
# discard uncommitted changes to a file
git restore code/02-clean.R

# unstage something you added by mistake
git restore --staged data/raw/big.csv

# go look at an old version without changing anything
git checkout abc123
git checkout main        # come back
```

--

<br>

Notice what is missing: nothing here rewrites history. Avoid `reset --hard` and force
pushes until you are confident. Committed work is very hard to lose; uncommitted work
is very easy to lose.

---

# Branches, minimally

You do not need elaborate branching for a solo project. You need one pattern:

--

```bash
git checkout -b robustness-alt-clustering
# ... try the thing ...
```

--

<br>

If it works: merge it back.
If it does not: `git checkout main` and the experiment never happened.

--

<br>

Use this when you want to try a specification you suspect you will abandon. It is
cheaper than commenting out forty lines and forgetting which ones.

---

# Working with coauthors

You will hit conflicts. They are not a crisis.

--

```bash
git pull                 # get their changes first, always
# ... conflict? git marks it in the file ...
# edit, keep what is right, then:
git add the-file.R
git commit
```

--

<br>

One rule that prevents most conflicts:

- **Pull before you start working**, not after you finish

---

# What NOT to commit

.large2[Never commit data. Never commit credentials.]

--

<br>

Data because it bloats the repo permanently, git keeps every version forever, so a
2GB CSV committed once is in your history for good, even if you delete it.

--

Credentials because a leaked API key, the secret token that lets your code call a
service, on a public repo gets scraped within *minutes*.
People run bots for exactly this.

--

<br>

Both are prevented by `.gitignore`, in two slides.

---

# GitHub for this course

Course material: https://github.com/dadepro/mkt699

--

<br>

**You create your own repository**, on your own account. Name it something real
`mkt699-project` is fine, `hw` is not.

--

<br>

Add me as a collaborator (`dadepro`) so I can see it. Private is fine.

It is yours after the semester ends, and some of these become papers (maybe).

---

# Submission

Your project repository **is** your submission. Not a zip file, not an email
attachment.

--

<br>

Send me the URL. I clone it and run it.

--

.large2[If it does not run from a clean clone, it does not run.]

--

<br>

Test this before you submit: clone your own repo into a fresh directory and run it.
You will be surprised how often it fails.

---

# `.gitignore` — do this now

```
# never commit data
data/raw/*
data/clean/*
!data/raw/.gitkeep

# never commit credentials
.Renviron
.env
*_key.txt

# noise
.Rhistory
.RData
.DS_Store
```

--

<br>

Write this file **first**, before your first commit. `.gitignore` only prevents future
mistakes. It does nothing about what you already committed.

---

# If you commit a key anyway

You will, or someone you work with will. What to do:

--

<br>

.large2[1. Revoke the key. Immediately.]

--

<br>

Not "remove it from the repo." **Revoke it at the provider.** Assume it is already
compromised, scrapers are faster than you are.

--

<br>

2. *Then* worry about cleaning history. In that order. Always.

---

# Keys go here instead

`.Renviron` in your project root (and in `.gitignore`):

```bash
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
```

--

Then in R:

```r
key <- Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
```

--

<br>

The key is never in a script, so it can never be committed, so it can never leak.
Your code becomes shareable by construction.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: shell

# The shell and remote computing

---

# Why the shell still matters

Some of you have never opened a terminal. That is fine, most PhD programs never
teach it, and then assume you know it.

--

<br>

The reason to learn it is not that syntax is hard. It is that the shell lets you
**inspect things without loading them into memory**.

--

<br>

Your 8GB CSV takes minutes to read into R. The shell answers "how many rows does it
have" in under a second.

---

# What the shell actually is

A program that reads a line you type, runs it, prints the result, and waits for the
next one.

--

<br>

Every command has the same shape:

```bash
command  -flags  arguments
```

--

```bash
ls              # command, no flags, no arguments
ls -l           # with a flag: "long" format
ls -l data/     # with a flag and an argument
```

--

<br>

That is the entire grammar. Everything you learn from here is vocabulary.

---

# Where am I?

The shell always has a **current directory**. Every relative path is interpreted from
there. Most beginner confusion is really "I was not where I thought I was."

--

```bash
pwd                    # print working directory — where am I?
ls                     # what is here?
cd data/raw            # go into a directory
cd ..                  # go UP one level
cd ~                   # go to my home directory
cd -                   # go back to where I just was
```

--

<br>

Type `pwd` whenever a command surprises you. It is the answer about half the time.

---

# Tab completion

The single highest-value keystroke on this slide.

--

```bash
cd data/ra<TAB>        # becomes cd data/raw/
```

--

<br>

Press `<TAB>` constantly. It completes file and directory names, which means:

- you type less
- you cannot typo a filename
- if it does not complete, **the file does not exist**. Which is itself the answer

--

<br>

Also: `↑` walks back through your previous commands. You will rarely retype anything.

---

# Looking at files

```bash
wc -l reviews.csv      # count lines: how many rows, actually?
head -3 reviews.csv    # first 3 lines: what are the columns?
tail -3 reviews.csv    # last 3 lines: did the file finish writing?
less reviews.csv       # scroll through it (q to quit)
```

--

<br>

`head` on a new dataset, always, before you write a single line of R.

--

You will catch: a header row that is actually data, a file that is
semicolon-separated, a "CSV" that is really tab-delimited, and an encoding problem.
All in one second, before R has told you a confusing lie about any of them.

---

# Files and space

```bash
ls -lh data/raw/       # list with human-readable sizes
du -sh data/raw/       # total size of a directory
df -h                  # how much disk space is left
```

--

<br>

`-h` means "human readable", `2.4G` instead of `2516582400`. It works on most
commands that print sizes.

--

<br>

`du -sh` before you start is how you find out whether this fits in RAM, or whether you
need DuckDB and a server.

---

# Did this file change?

```bash
md5 data/raw/reviews.csv        # macOS
md5sum data/raw/reviews.csv     # Linux (our servers)
```

--

Prints a fingerprint of the file's contents. Same contents, same fingerprint. One byte
different, completely different fingerprint.

--

<br>

.large2[When your results shift, the first question is always: did the data change, or
did the code change?]

---

# You do not memorise the checksum

You write it down once, and let the machine do the comparing.

```bash
# Once, when you first pull the data
md5 -r data/raw/*.csv > data/raw/CHECKSUMS.txt
```

--

```bash
# Any time later
md5 -r data/raw/*.csv | diff - data/raw/CHECKSUMS.txt && echo "unchanged"
```

--

<br>

Silence means nothing moved. Any output names the file that did.

--

.small[On Linux use `md5sum` in place of `md5 -r`, and `md5sum -c CHECKSUMS.txt` to
check.]

---

# Finding things

```bash
grep "sarcasm" prompts/*.md         # which prompt files mention this?
grep -r "cluster" code/             # search recursively through a directory
grep -c "error" logs/annotate.log   # count matches instead of printing them
```

--

<br>

```bash
find . -name "*.parquet"            # where did that file go?
find . -name "*.csv" -size +100M    # find the big ones
```

--

<br>

`grep` searches *inside* files. `find` searches *for* files. That is the distinction
people mix up.

---

# Pipes: the one big idea

`|` takes the output of one command and feeds it as input to the next.

--

```bash
head -1 reviews.csv | tr ',' '\n' | wc -l
```

--

<br>

Read it left to right:

1. `head -1`, take the header row
2. `tr ',' '\n'`, turn every comma into a newline
3. `wc -l`, count the lines

--

.large2[**How many columns does this file have?**]

--

Small tools, chained. That is the whole design philosophy.

---

# A pipe you will actually use

Which cities appear in this file, and how often?

```bash
tail -n +2 reviews.csv | cut -d',' -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
```

--

.small90[
```
 482913 Los Angeles
 291044 San Diego
 118220 San Francisco
     17 los angeles      # <-- there it is
```
]

--

<br>

You just found an inconsistent-capitalization bug that would have silently split a
city into two groups in your regression. In one line, before loading anything.

---

# Redirecting output

```bash
Rscript code/03-measure.R > logs/run.log        # send output to a file
Rscript code/03-measure.R > logs/run.log 2>&1   # errors too
Rscript code/03-measure.R >> logs/run.log       # append, don't overwrite
```

--

<br>

`>` overwrites. `>>` appends. `2>&1` means "send errors to the same place as normal
output."

--

<br>

Do this for every long job. When your annotation run dies at hour six, the log is the
only evidence of why.

---

# Getting help

```bash
man wc           # the manual page (q to quit)
wc --help        # shorter version
```

--

<br>

Honestly? Ask a model. "What does `sort -rn` do?" gets you a better answer than `man
sort`, faster.

--

<br>

The shell is one of the things LLMs are genuinely excellent at, because the commands
are short, well-documented, and have been discussed on the internet for forty years.

--

Learn the *concepts* here. Look up the flags forever.

---

# A warning

`rm` deletes. There is no trash, no undo, no "are you sure."

--

```bash
rm file.csv          # gone
rm -r directory/     # gone, with everything in it
```

--

<br>

Be especially careful with `rm -rf` and wildcards. `rm -rf *` in the wrong directory
is how people lose a chapter.

--

<br>

This is also why `data/raw/` is read-only and why everything is in git. Not paranoia
just the recognition that you will eventually run the wrong command in the wrong
directory at 2am.

---

# Our servers

You have two machines for this course. Addresses handed out in class, put them in your
`.Renviron` or `~/.ssh/config` as `mkt699a` and `mkt699b`.

```bash
ssh mkt699a
```

--

<br>

You must be on a **USC network or the USC VPN** to reach them. These are internal
addresses; they do not resolve from a coffee shop.

---

# Why you need them

Annotating 200k reviews takes hours. Sometimes a day.

--

<br>

You do not want that job on your laptop, because your laptop closes, sleeps, runs out
of battery, and goes home with you.

--

<br>

.large2[A measurement pipeline that has to be restarted four times is a measurement
pipeline that never finishes.]

---

# Connecting

```bash
ssh you@mkt699a
```

--

Move files with `scp` or, better, `rsync`:

```bash
rsync -avz data/raw/ you@mkt699a:~/project/data/raw/
```

--

<br>

`rsync` only transfers what changed. When you are moving 40GB of scraped HTML for the
third time, this matters.

---

# The thing that actually saves you: `tmux`

```bash
ssh you@mkt699a
tmux new -s annotate

# start your annotation job
Rscript code/03-measure.R

# Ctrl-b, then d   -> detach. job keeps running.
# ... close laptop, go home, sleep ...

ssh you@mkt699a
tmux attach -t annotate     # still going
```

---

# Two servers, one warning

Pick one and stay on it for a given project.

--

<br>

Your data is on the machine you put it on. There is no shared filesystem between them.

--

<br>

Put the server name in your README.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: env

# Environments and dependencies

---

# The problem

Your code works. Six months later a referee asks you to rerun it. It does not work.

--

Something upgraded. A package changed a default. `data.table` deprecated something.
A function you relied on was removed.

--

<br>

This was always annoying. It is now worse, because **model APIs change too**, and
unlike a package, you cannot pin a model version forever.

---

# R: `renv`

Three commands, and you will use them in this order.

--

```r
renv::init()       # once, at the start of a project
```

Creates a project-local library and an `.Rprofile` so R uses it automatically. Packages
you install now belong to *this project*, not your machine.

--

```r
renv::snapshot()   # whenever you add or update a package
```

Writes `renv.lock`.

---

# What `renv.lock` looks like

```json
{
  "R": { "Version": "4.6.0",
         "Repositories": [ { "Name": "CRAN",
           "URL": "https://cloud.r-project.org" } ] },
  "Packages": {
    "data.table": {
      "Package": "data.table",
      "Version": "1.18.4",
      "Source": "Repository",
      ...
```

--

<br>

R version, repository, and an exact version for every package. **Commit this file.**

---

# The payoff

```r
renv::restore()    # on a new machine, or in two years
```

--

<br>

Reads the lockfile and installs precisely those versions. Your coauthor runs one command
and has your environment.

--

<br>

.small90[`renv::status()` tells you when your library and lockfile have drifted apart,
which happens the moment you install something and forget to snapshot.]

---

# Python: `uv`

`uv` installs Python itself and manages your project's packages. One tool in place of
`pip`, `venv`, and `pyenv`.

--

```bash
uv init                          # once, at the start of a project
```

Creates `pyproject.toml` and pins a Python version in `.python-version`.

--

```bash
uv add polars
#  + polars==1.36.1
#  + polars-runtime-32==1.36.1
```

Installs it, records it in `pyproject.toml`, and writes `uv.lock`.

---

# The two files `uv` gives you

**`pyproject.toml`** is what you asked for:

```toml
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.9"
dependencies = [
    "polars>=1.36.1",
]
```

--

**`uv.lock`** is what you got: every transitive dependency at an exact version, including
the ones you never named. Commit both.

---

# Running things

```bash
uv run python 03-measure.py
```

`uv run` executes inside the project environment. No activating, no wondering which
Python you are on.

--

<br>

And the payoff, the same as `renv::restore()`:

```bash
uv sync            # rebuild the environment from uv.lock
```

--

<br>

.small90[One asymmetry worth knowing: `uv` installs Python itself, so `uv sync` gets your
coauthor the right interpreter too. `renv` does not install R.]

---

# The part that is genuinely unsolved

You cannot `renv::snapshot()` a model.

--

<br>

`claude-sonnet-4-5` today and `claude-sonnet-4-5` in eighteen months may not be the same
artifact. Providers deprecate model versions. Behavior drifts.

--

<br>

**What you can do:**

- Record the exact model string and the date accessed
- Save the raw model outputs, not just the derived variable
- Keep your validation sample, so a future you can re-validate

--

That third one is the important one. If you saved the gold-standard labels, you can
re-run the measurement with a new model and check whether your conclusions survive.

---

name: ai

# Setting up your AI workflow

---

# We are all using VS Code

I am standardizing the class on **VS Code**. Install it before next week.

https://code.visualstudio.com

--

<br>

You may already have a setup you like, RStudio, Jupyter, PyCharm, Emacs. Keep it for
your own work if you want.

---

# Why VS Code specifically

Because it is the one editor that does **all** of this at once:

--

- **R** and **Python** in the same window, same project
- An integrated **terminal**: the shell we just covered, no separate app
- **Git** built in: stage, diff, and commit visually while you learn the commands
- **Remote-SSH**: edit files *on our servers* as if they were local
- Native home for **coding agents**

--

<br>

That fourth one is the reason. You are going to be working on the servers a lot.

---

# Extensions to install

In VS Code, open Extensions (`Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+X`) and install:

--

.small90[
| Extension | What it gives you |
|:--|:--|
| **R** (REditorSupport) | R language support, run code in a terminal |
| **Python** (Microsoft) | Python, notebooks, environments |
| **Remote - SSH** | Work directly on our servers |
| **Quarto** | Reproducible documents for assignments |
| **Claude Code** *(or your agent)* | The coding agent, in the editor |
]

---

# Remote-SSH is the one to learn

```
Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P  ->  "Remote-SSH: Connect to Host"
                  ->  you@mkt699a
```

--

<br>

Now VS Code is running *on the server*. Your files, your terminal, your agent, all
there. The editor just happens to be displayed on your laptop.

--

<br>

.large2[This is how you work on data that will never fit on your laptop.]

--

No more editing locally, `scp`-ing up, running, `scp`-ing results back, and losing
track of which copy is current.

---

# The three things you need

**1. An editor.** VS Code. Settled.

--

**2. A coding agent.** Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, all run inside VS Code.

I use Claude Code for most of my own work. Use what you like, but it
must be an agent that reads your **whole repo**, not a chat window you paste into.

--

**3. API access.** For the Week 4–5 measurement pipeline.

--

<br>

A ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro subscription does
**not** give you an API key. They are separate products, billed separately.

---

# The cost question

You will be making tens of thousands of API calls for your project.

--

Rough orders of magnitude for annotation with a mid-tier model:

- 10k short documents: a few dollars
- 200k short documents: tens of dollars
- Long documents with reasoning: multiply by 10–50

--

<br>

This is cheap relative to hiring RAs. That is the entire reason this literature exists.

But it is **not free**, and a runaway loop can burn real money. We will cover batching,
caching, and rate limiting in Week 3.

--

In this class, we will spend a 10s of dollars and you can use your own budget. But let me know if you are concerned about cost, and we will cover it.

---

# A warning I want to give early

The tools are good. They will make you fast.

--

<br>

They will also make you fast at being **wrong**, and they will do it in a way that feels
exactly like being right.

--

<br>

There is no phenomenological difference between reading correct model output and
reading confidently incorrect model output. None. The subjective experience is
identical.

--

<br>

.large2[The only defense is process.]

That is what next week is about.

---

# Next week

**AI-assisted analysis and the verification problem.**

We spend the session on failure modes: silent merge errors, sample-selection changes,
misapplied clustering, fabricated variable definitions, hallucinated citations.

--

<br>

**In-class lab:** I will hand you a complete analysis produced by an AI agent from a
dirty dataset. It runs. It produces a clean table. It is wrong in at least six ways.

Find them.

---

# Before next class

1. **Create your repository** on your own GitHub account, using the structure from
   today. Add `dadepro` as a collaborator and send me the URL.

2. **Install** VS Code (with the extensions above), R, Python (using `uv`), git, and a
   coding agent.

3. **Log in to a server** (either one) and start a `tmux`
   session. Just prove to yourself you can do it.

4. **Get API access** to at least one model provider.

5. **Start thinking about your question.** Week 2 milestone is one paragraph. Come with
   two or three candidates and we will talk about which is feasible.

---
